source.title: Training Compute-Optimal Vision Transformers for Brain Encoding
source.authors: Sana Ahmadi; François Paugam; Tristan Glatard; P. Bellec

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies training-data and model configurations for a video transformer in a brain-encoding task, extending scaling-related evaluation to a vision/video setting. It reports downstream prediction outcomes, but does not fit or test the language-model loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training cross-entropy curves and brain-encoding correlations. The former are training losses, not held-out pretraining losses; the latter are downstream brain-encoding measures. It does not report fitted power laws, large-run extrapolation, or a fixed-compute allocation experiment.
record.test_reason: The study varies training-set size (10K to 6M) and GPT width/depth for a VideoGPT, then scores a downstream readout: ridge brain-encoding correlation on held-out fMRI. That bears on V6 in a new setting (video transformer, brain encoding). It fits no power laws, reports only training loss rather than held-out loss, and runs no compute-allocation experiment, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that data scaling helps brain encoding more than model scaling. Width helps up to 576, with diminishing returns or overfitting beyond. Depth has a limited, inconsistent effect: their 'gains up to eight layers' refers to training loss, while for most subjects encoding peaks at 1 layer. Head count has little impact, and FP16 matches FP32 at 1.17× speed.
record.recipe_differences: This is a video-transformer brain-encoding benchmark, not a language-model held-out-loss scaling-law fit; it varies training sample count and model configuration and evaluates ridge-regression brain-encoding correlations.
record.method_sensitivity: Brain-encoding correlations vary by participant and configuration: dataset-size gains differ across subjects; hidden-dimension results fluctuate, with declines at dimension 126 and some declines at 1024; layer-count gains are inconsistent; head-count effects differ by subject.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT training cross-entropy generally falls with more data and larger width. It plateaus beyond 4 layers and rises slightly late in training at 1024 width, at 16 layers and on 100K samples. Head count leaves training loss unchanged. No held-out loss and no fit are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a small VideoGPT, training loss falls with data and width but shows overfitting at the largest settings. Head count does not affect loss.

record.problems: Only four participants are included. Most per-condition brain-encoding values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper's losses are training losses rather than held-out losses; it does not fit scaling exponents or evaluate fixed-compute optimality. The text inconsistently describes the head-count conditions: the method gives 1, 4, and 8 heads, while one result mentions 2 heads.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's figures separately show further brain-encoding correlations for dataset sizes 100K and 1M, additional hidden dimensions, and several per-subject configuration values. These plotted per-subject results were not individually extracted beyond the text-described comparisons, to keep the record within the 60-row limit and avoid assigning untranscribed plot values. Training-loss curves are recorded as aggregate text descriptions rather than separate rows for each training condition.

untested.parts: Whether the improvement is predictable: no fitted trend or extrapolation. Any link between pretraining (held-out) loss and downstream score. Scale beyond roughly 76M parameters. 100K and 1M data points are shown only in a figure.
No held-out loss and no power-law fit. Training-loss curves only.
A video model is trained, but no power-law form is fitted to its loss.
Head count leaves training loss unchanged (r24), but this is training loss, in video, for one shape dimension only. It is not tested as V4.

missing.what: Brain-encoding correlations at 100K and 1M samples, needed to judge whether the data-scaling trend is monotonic or predictable. Declared in rows_left_out but not shown numerically.
Per-subject width correlations at 15, 63 and 255 dimensions.

record.verdict_notes: Small study: four subjects, models of about 76M parameters, mostly figure-only values, and no uncertainty reported. The only V6 link is to brain encoding as a downstream readout from a video model, not an LM benchmark. The depth comparison is confounded because a different extraction layer is used per depth (Table 3). The text says 'six subjects' in Section 3.5 but the dataset has four.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss law in parameters, tokens, or compute is tested.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run held-out loss.
No fixed-compute budget or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
The study measures brain-encoding correlations, not held-out pretraining loss as architecture details change.
Although it uses a video model, it does not test whether the same power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.

The study tests brain-encoding prediction correlations under selected model and dataset changes, but not downstream task predictability across many orders of scale or as a function of pretraining loss.
It does not examine fitted exponents, fit choices, or departures from a fitted power law.

relationships.condition: Data scaling 10K→6M for Sub-01 and Sub-06; hidden dimension up to 576 for Sub-01, Sub-04 and Sub-06
relationships.reason: Correlation rises 0.4→0.6 (Sub-01) and 0.15→0.55 (Sub-06) with more data, and is highest at hidden dim 576 (r2, r4, r9).
relationships.display_finding: With more data, prediction correlations rise from 0.4 to 0.6 for Sub-01 and 0.15 to 0.55 for Sub-06, while hidden dimension 576 yields the highest correlations in the specified dimension sweeps.

relationships.condition: Sub-02 data scaling; non-monotonic width results; depth gain only for Sub-02
relationships.reason: Sub-02 gains only 1.14×. Width shows a drop at 30 for Sub-02, a drop for all subjects at 126, and declines at 1024. Only Sub-02 improves with 2 layers (r6, r7, r8, r10, r12).
relationships.display_finding: Sub-02 gained only 1.14× from data scaling, width increases produced declines at 30 for Sub-02 and at 126 for all subjects plus declines at 1024, and only Sub-02 improved with two layers.

relationships.condition: Depth scaling (1→8 layers) for Sub-01, Sub-04 and Sub-06
relationships.reason: The text states the 1-layer model gives the highest correlations for these subjects. Caveat: the extraction layer differs by depth (r11, r13, r14).
relationships.display_finding: The 1-layer model achieved the highest correlations for all three subjects, although the feature-extraction layer changed with model depth.
